info.bio:
Rock de fusión originaria de los Estados Unidos, caracterizada por una amplia fusión de diversos estilos: ska, funk, punk rock, reggae y heavy metal.

La banda nació en 1979, fundada por su ya mítico líder y vocalista Angelo Moore, en los barrios de Los Angeles, California. El grupo nació en la misma zona de donde salieron artistas y bandas del calibre de Red Hot Chili Peppers y Jane's Addiction.

scenes.name: Black rock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: «El funk es blues acelerado» (Clinton). Pese a Chuck Berry, Little Richard o Bo Diddley, el rock se volvió una forma blanca y la invasión británica reforzó el mito, aunque sus grupos venían del blues negro. Hendrix y Sly lo desmontaron a finales de los sesenta, pero la industria resegregó el rock en pocos años, hasta Prince. El blues eléctrico (Muddy Waters, con su «gran caída tras el golpe del tambor») tuvo su revival ante el público blanco. En la Costa Oeste, multirracial y lejos de los problemas del Norte y del Sur, florecieron bandas mestizas (Sly, Tower of Power, Santana): la influencia del rock psicodélico convirtió el funk de un R&B salvaje en algo universal. A mediados de los setenta el black rock se convirtió en funk, porque la radio obligó a quitar los solos de guitarra; solo algunos resistieron («Who Says a Funk Band Can’t Play Rock?!» de Funkadelic, Slave, Mother’s Finest, los Isley) hasta Prince y la Black Rock Coalition de Vernon Reid (1985), y en los noventa Living Colour, Body Count, Bad Brains o Fishbone.

scenes.name: Funk rock: Chili Peppers, Primus y la Black Rock Coalition
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: A los blancos les era mucho más fácil tocar funk y grabar: Jane’s Addiction debutó con un directo, Primus de Les Claypool (devoto de Larry Graham), los Limbomaniacs con Bootsy y Maceo, Praxis. Los Red Hot Chili Peppers de Anthony Kiedis y Flea, con Freaky Styley producido por Clinton (1985), versionaron a Sly, los Meters y Stevie y llevaron a P-Funk al escenario de los Grammy de 1993; pero los creadores del funk rock, como los P-Funk All Stars, no tenían esa libertad. En Nueva York Living Colour de Vernon Reid no conseguía contrato pese a tener a Mick Jagger de fan, y Reid y Greg Tate fundaron en 1985 la Black Rock Coalition: «El rock and roll es música negra y nosotros somos sus herederos», contra el «rock de orientación apartheid». Abrió paso a Steve Coleman, Me’Shell NdegéOcello, James Blood Ulmer o el Kelvynator de Kelvyn Bell.

scenes.name: Funk-metal
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Una de las grandes ideas de fusión de los ochenta: integrar los ritmos y voces brutales del funk y el rap con el metal de guitarras. Los Red Hot Chili Peppers descubren lo que tenían en común George Clinton y Jello Biafra; Fishbone y su fusión satírica de funk, ska y soul; Faith No More, híbrido inventivo de punk, funk, progresivo, hip hop y metal (Introduce Yourself, Angel Dust); Victim's Family.

mentions.text: …scene was going through a painful rehabilitation program. A milder and more satirical approach to funk-ska-soul-rock fusion was propounded by Fishbone (2). The best document of their frantic, exuberant, exhilarating style was their debut EP, Fishbone (1985). Fishbone continued a tradition that dated as far back as the Coasters and had survived via Madness. That party music modeled after high-school pranks grew…

podcast.title: Pioneers of Genre Blending (1979)
podcast.body: Fishbone formed in 1979 in South Central LA with four black members, becoming highly important for blending punk and funk, along with ska, hard rock, soul, and elements of hip hop and rap. "They were formed in 1979, four black guys from South Central LA. Their stuff was socially conscious, anti-racist, clever, witty, and basically a lot of fun."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peak Years (1988-1994)
podcast.body: The band's most commercially and critically successful period was between 1988 and 1994, after which their career encountered various difficulties. "Fishbone's best years were from 1988 to about 1994, and then things got kind of weird."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring with Beastie Boys and Lollapalooza 1993
podcast.body: Fishbone opened for the Beastie Boys on tour and was a main stage performer at the 1993 Lollapalooza tour, showcasing their widespread recognition. "the Beastie Boys would tag fishbone to open one of their tours, and they were one of the main stage performers on the 1993 La Lava Pulusa tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Booked for Content Pivot (1996)
podcast.body: Fishbone was one of the bands booked for the 1996 Warped Tour as the festival pivoted its content from broad-range alternative to focus on punk and other music that complemented skate culture, following its sponsorship by Vans. "This meant booking fishbone, the muddy, muddy boss tones, no effect, 3-11 penny wise, and this weird new group from San Diego called Blink 182."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: $1.4 Million Settlement for Stage Diving Injury (2014)
podcast.body: In 2014, Fishbone was required to pay $1.4 million to a woman who sustained a broken collarbone when the band's Angelo Moore stage-dived on top of her. This incident underscored the serious legal and financial consequences of stage diving for bands and highlighted the need for greater audience safety. "That same year, fishbone had to pay $1.4 million to a woman who was hurt with a band's Angelo Moore staged over on top of her, breaking her collarbone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bridge to the Third Wave
podcast.body: Fishbone is credited with serving as vital connective tissue between the second wave of Ska in the late 1970s and early 1980s and the emergence of the third wave. They became an important part of the West Coast alternative scene, making serious inroads to Alt Rock by 1988 and stirring the beginnings of the third wave. "A band that served as vital connective tissue between the second wave of SCAT in the very late 70s and the early 80s and what was to come with the third wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Growth to Six Members
podcast.body: The band initially started with four members and later expanded to six, playing alongside various punk bands. "Soon there were six of them, and they were playing alongside punk bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Flea's Bassline
podcast.body: Flea from Red Hot Chili Peppers was working on a side project called Hate with members of the punk-funk band Fishbone when he developed the bassline for "Give It Away." "Lee came up with the bass line while working on a side project called Hate with a few members of the punk-funk band Fishbone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Red Hot Chili Peppers
podcast.body: Fishbone was highly admired by a group that eventually coalesced into the Red Hot Chili Peppers, highlighting their early impact. "There was this one particular group that loved fishbone and what they were doing, and they eventually coalesced into something called the Red Hot Chili Peppers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influenced Notable Bands
podcast.body: Fishbone holds a fanatical following and is cited as an important influence by a long list of bands, including Sublime, 311, Goldfinger, Rage Against the Machine, and Faith No More. "No doubt. Sublime. 311. Goldfinger. Rage Against The Machine. Faith No More."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Member Joining Religious Cult
podcast.body: One member of Fishbone quit the band to join a religious cult, and another member who attempted to extract him from the cult was subsequently charged with attempted kidnapping. "One member quit to join a religious cult, and when another member tried to break him out, that guy was charged with attempted kidnapping."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Philadelphia Lawsuit ($1.4 Million)
podcast.body: The band faced a lawsuit from a woman in Philadelphia, who successfully sued them for $1.4 million after one of the members "staged a Dove on Top of Her," contributing to their personnel and record company issues. "They had record company issues, and they were sued by a woman in Philadelphia after one of the members staged a Dove on Top of Her. That was good for $1.4 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Socially Conscious and Anti-Racist Message
podcast.body: Their music was characterized by socially conscious, anti-racist, clever, and witty lyrics, contributing to their unique and fun sound. "Their stuff was socially conscious, anti-racist, clever, witty, and basically a lot of fun."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lollapalooza (1991) Headliner
xref.body: Jane's Addiction headlined the very first Lollapalooza show, which began outside Phoenix on July 18, 1991. The festival was originally conceived as their farewell tour. "The lineup featured Jane's addiction, Susie in the bandsheets, living color, nine inch nails, butthole, surfers, raw on-span, iced tea and body count, and fishbone."

xref.title: All-Black Funk Metal Band
xref.body: Living Color emerged as an all-black funk metal band around the time Fishbone was peaking, fusing funk and metal in their sound. "along came Living Color, an All Black Funk Metal Band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Emergence from Fishbone Influence
xref.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers coalesced from a group that admired and was influenced by Fishbone's music and approach. "There was this one particular group that loved fishbone and what they were doing, and they eventually coalesced into something called the Red Hot Chili Peppers."
